title: Riemann Sum
body:
The construction the definite [[Integral]] is **defined as**, before anyone shows you a shortcut.
To find the area under $f$ on $[a,b]$: chop the interval into $n$ strips of width
$\Delta x = \frac{b-a}{n}$, approximate each strip by a rectangle, and add.

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} f(x_i^*)\,\Delta x
\qquad\xrightarrow{\;n \to \infty\;}\qquad
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx
$$

```
 |    ____                    |  ▄▄▄▄
 |   /    \                   | ███████
 |  /      \        ~~~>      |█████████
 |_/________\_                |█████████
 a            b               a         b
   true area                    n rectangles
```

$x_i^*$ is the sample point in strip $i$, and the choice gives the named variants: **left**
endpoint, **right** endpoint, and **midpoint** sums. Left and right bracket the answer for a
monotonic function, midpoint is usually the most accurate of the three, and in the limit they all
agree, which is the point.

The $\int$ sign is a stretched S for "sum" and the $dx$ is the $\Delta x$ after the limit. The
notation is a picture of this construction, not a decoration.

## Why bother, given the shortcut exists

The [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]] makes almost every integral in the course a two-line
subtraction, so the sums look like a hazing ritual. Two reasons they are not:

1. **This is the definition.** The FTC is a theorem *about* it, and it needs an antiderivative to
   exist and be findable. When one is not (as for $e^{-x^2}$), the sum is what remains, and every
   numerical integration method a computer runs (trapezoid, Simpson's, Monte Carlo) is a Riemann
   sum with a better choice of rectangle.
2. **It is where the generalisations come from.** "Chop, approximate each piece by something
   simple, add, take a limit" is the move that produces arc length, volume, work, centre of mass,
   and expectation, each with a different thing in the sum. Recognising an accumulation as a
   Riemann sum is how you know which integral to write down.

The link to [[Average Value]] and [[STATISTICS]] is the same observation: $E[X] = \int x f(x)\,dx$
is a weighted sum where the weights have been taken to a continuum. A discrete expectation
$\sum x_i p_i$ *is* a Riemann sum of the continuous one.

## Related

- [[Limit]]: the operation being taken, and the reason the answer is exact rather than approximate
- [[Integral]], [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]]
- [[CALCULUS 1]]
- [[CALCULUS 2]] is where point 2 above gets cashed in, one note per choice of slice:
  [[Solids of Revolution]] (a disk or a shell), [[Arc Length]] (a hypotenuse),
  [[Applications of Integration]] (work, pressure, centre of mass), [[Polar Coordinates]] (a
  circular sector), and [[Double Integral]] (a box). Same construction every time, and recognising
  which slice the problem wants is the only real decision
